moments.title: I went down the rabbit hole: Anthropic is already being sued over exactly this. And the $200 plan really only provides only around 2x the weekly usage of the $100 plan Here is where the confusion comes from. Anthropic’s
moments.selftext: I went down the rabbit hole: Anthropic is already being sued over exactly this. And the $200 plan really only provides only around 2x the weekly usage of the $100 plan Here is where the confusion comes from. Anthropic’s pricing page says: “Choose 5x or 20x more usage than Pro.” That naturally makes the $200 Max 20x plan sound like it includes four times the usage of the $100 Max 5x plan. Only further down does Anthropic clarify: “Max gives you 5x or 20x more usage per 5-hour session than Pro.” Those multipliers do not apply to the separate weekly caps, whose exact size Anthropic does not disclose. A proposed class action filed in June alleges that Max 5x delivers around 3.5x Pro’s weekly usage, while Max 20x delivers just 6–8x. In practice, the $200 plan therefore provides only around 2x the weekly usage of the $100 plan, sometimes even less depending on the model. The “20x” is real within each five-hour window. The weekly limit makes the overall offer look very different. h/t @Hesamation for finding the original court files first i think

moments.title: “Whenever you find yourself on the side of the majority, it is time to pause and reflect.” - Mark Twain Mark Twain wrote this thought in his notebook in 1904. It reflected a recurring theme in his later writing: his dist
moments.selftext: “Whenever you find yourself on the side of the majority, it is time to pause and reflect.” - Mark Twain Mark Twain wrote this thought in his notebook in 1904. It reflected a recurring theme in his later writing: his distrust of conformity and the tendency to accept ideas simply because everyone else does. Twain wasn’t arguing that the majority is always wrong. His point was simpler: popularity does not make something true. When almost everyone agrees, it may be worth asking yourself why you agree, too.

moments.title: BREAKING: Sweden’s Infrastructure Minister and senior citizens just experienced Tesla FSD. 🇸🇪 Andreas Carlson posted a video showing the Tesla steering through town and turning by itself. He attended a Tesla FSD demonstr
moments.selftext: BREAKING: Sweden’s Infrastructure Minister and senior citizens just experienced Tesla FSD. 🇸🇪 Andreas Carlson posted a video showing the Tesla steering through town and turning by itself. He attended a Tesla FSD demonstration at the Margaretas Park elder-care home in Mullsjö, where he rode alongside senior citizen. Other elderly residents also experienced the technology, and their feedback was highly positive. “It felt like riding with a person.” He described the experience as very interesting and great fun, adding that the trained safety driver did not touch the controls during his ride. “I view this as a helpful tool, especially for older people.” He said the technology could help people who need a way to get around and compared the experience to sitting in the back seat while someone else drives. Another senior said the ride went well, including on the main road and through a roundabout. Mullsjö now wants to become a pilot municipality for future robotaxis, with the goal of giving seniors greater access to transportation. Sweden currently permits Tesla to conduct limited FSD tests with trained drivers on selected routes. Consumer activation is not yet approved. Source: SVT, Sveriges Radio and Transportstyrelsen.

moments.title: The assembly line for the SR-71 Blackbird at Lockheed Martin’s Advanced Development Programs, better known as “Skunk Works,” in 1965. In 1965, SR-71 Blackbirds were being assembled at Lockheed’s highly secretive Skunk Wo
moments.selftext: The assembly line for the SR-71 Blackbird at Lockheed Martin’s Advanced Development Programs, better known as “Skunk Works,” in 1965. In 1965, SR-71 Blackbirds were being assembled at Lockheed’s highly secretive Skunk Works facility in Burbank, California. The aircraft had completed its first flight on December 22, 1964, and production continued behind tight security, just a few hundred feet from the Hollywood Freeway. Built primarily from titanium and its alloys, the SR-71 was designed to withstand the extreme heat generated during sustained flight above Mach 3. Lockheed ultimately produced 32 Blackbirds, including two-seat trainer versions. Designed by legendary Skunk Works engineer Clarence “Kelly” Johnson, the SR-71 became one of the most remarkable reconnaissance aircraft of the Cold War. It could cruise above 80,000 feet at more than three times the speed of sound, allowing its two-person crews to collect photographic and electronic intelligence over vast areas. The Blackbird entered U.S. Air Force service in 1966 and went on to establish numerous speed and altitude records. In 1976, it reached an absolute speed record of 2,193.2 mph, a mark that remains one of aviation’s most famous achievements.
